source_text: Magnis licet impeditus angoribus, quos intuenti mihi hac tempestate Ecclesiarum statum, partim indignatio ingerit, partim miseratio; non abieceram tamen promissionis meae fidem, videlicet ut qui fueram factus debitor promittendo, solvendo quoque esse curarem. Nam in libris quos ad fratrem nostrum Turbantium episcopum, virum magno virtutum fulgore conspicuum, contra Augustini scripta dictavi, pollicitus sum, si nihil quod studiis obsisteret, eveniret incommodi, occursurum me protinus eorum argumentis omnibus, qui ex sententia Manichaeorum traducem peccati, id est malum naturale defenderent; a quo sum hactenus munere varia et indissimulabili necessitate suspensus.
pass_a_gloss: Although hindered by great distresses, which, as I look at the state of the Churches in this season, indignation in part inflicts, pity in part; I had nevertheless not thrown away the faith of my promise, namely that I who had been made a debtor by promising should take care to be one also by paying. For in the books which I dictated to our brother bishop Turbantius, a man conspicuous by the great brightness of virtues, against Augustine's writings, I promised that, if no inconvenience should occur that would stand against studies, I would at once meet all the arguments of those who, from the opinion of the Manichaeans, were defending the tradux of sin, that is a natural evil; from which office I have until now been hung back by various and undisguisable necessity.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice

pass_b_english: Although I was burdened with great distress, stirred partly by indignation and partly by pity as I looked at the condition of the churches in these times, I had not abandoned my pledge. Having made myself a debtor by promising, I meant to take care to pay that debt as well. In the books I dictated against Augustine's writings, addressed to our brother Bishop Turbantius, a man distinguished by the great brilliance of his virtues, I promised that, unless some obstacle to my studies arose, I would immediately answer all the arguments of those who, following the opinion of the Manichaeans, defended the transmission of sin by descent, that is, an evil inherent in nature. Various pressing circumstances, which cannot honestly be ignored, have kept me from that task until now.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
